After the '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.manipulation.cvel2.html#casatasks.manipulation.cvel2 cvel2]''' step and imaged with '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.imaging.tclean.html#casatasks.imaging.tclean tclean]''' using parameter ''specmode='cubedata' '' to conserve the velocity system and grid. Note that '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.manipulation.cvel2.html#casatasks.manipulation.cvel2 cvel2]''' can also Hanning smooth the data if needed (as an alternative to the stand-alone '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.manipulation.hanningsmooth.html#casatasks.manipulation.hanningsmooth hanningsmooth]''' task).

==Image the Spectral Line Data==

The step above was for information purposes, for the tutorial we now go back to the split off data of the target source IRC+10216. This is the measurement set ''irc10216.ms.contsub'' which for the purposes of this guide we have stored in the variable ''vis_contsub''. Since imaging can generally be a computationally intensive and time consuming task, especially for images with high angular resolution (i.e., many pixels) and many channels, it is generally good practice to first explore a limited selection of channels and then expand the analysis when we have a good idea of how best to proceed. Thus our imaging strategy is to (1) first image a few channels containing emission to assess, (2) image a few off-line channels to estimate the image noise, (3) interactively CLEAN a few channels with emission that we can use a reference, (4) apply automated imaging techniques to a few channels and compare their quality to the manually cleaned version from step-4, and finally (5) apply the automated techniques to the full cube. While our dataset is small and is in practice straightforward to image completely interactively from the start, these steps are meant to be a guide for more realistic, larger line imaging tasks that would be prohibitive to image manually (e.g., long tracks, multiple configurations, many spectral windows, many targets, etc.).

If you are starting mid-way through the guide using a measurement set that has already been calibrated, then these variables need to be assigned for the following commands to work correctly:

<source lang="python">
field_target = "IRC+10216"
vis_contsub = "irc10216.ms.contsub"
</source>

===Creating a dirty image===

We start by imaging a couple channels where emission is expected to be present to get a sense of how bright and extended the emission is. For other datasets, we may be concerned with whether emission is detected at all, although from the plot of amplitude versus channel (Figure 21) we know that strong emission is present from the get-go. We pick channel indices 18 and 19 for spectral window index 1 (HC3N), as they are especially bright in the averaged ''uv''-data.

For imaging we will use the CASA task '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.imaging.tclean.html#casatasks.imaging.tclean tclean]''' to deconvolve the data. We'll start by generating a dirty map, i.e., one before any deconvolution has been applied and thus will contain significant artifacts from the sidelobes and structure of the synthesized beam. But, by having an image on hand before we attempt to interactively CLEAN, we can better assess the imaging parameters such as the image pixel size (''cell'' size), size of the image (''imsize''), how far out to extend the primary beam mask, and other important quantities.

'''Note that interrupting [https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.imaging.tclean.html#casatasks.imaging.tclean tclean] by Ctrl+C or by closing the viewer window may corrupt your visibilities or your CASA session when setting the parameter ''savemodel='modelcolumn' '' in 'tclean', as this option requires writing to the model column of the measurement set.'''

If '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.manipulation.cvel2.html#casatasks.manipulation.cvel2 cvel2]''' task was used in a previous step, then set the parameter specmode='cubedata', otherwise leave specmode='cube' within the '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.imaging.tclean.html#casatasks.imaging.tclean tclean]''' task.

Below we create a dirty image by calling ''tclean'' with zero minor cycle iterations by setting ''niter=0'' such that it halts immediately after the image is created. The [http://casaguides.nrao.edu/index.php/VLA_CASA_Imaging VLA Imaging topical guide] has more information on the settings of the individual parameters of ''tclean''. We also set variables for the line rest frequencies as a convenience.

<source lang="python">
restfreq_hc3n = "36.392238GHz"
restfreq_sis  = "36.309627GHz"

imagename_dirty = f"{field_target}_HC3N_dirty"
rmtables(f"{imagename_dirty}.*")
tclean(
    vis=vis_contsub,
    spw="1",
    imagename=imagename_dirty,
    imsize=[300, 300],
    cell="0.4arcsec",
    specmode="cube",
    outframe="LSRK",
    start=18,
    nchan=2,
    restfreq=restfreq_hc3n,
    perchanweightdensity=True,
    pblimit=-0.001,
    weighting="briggs",
    robust=0.5,
    niter=0,
    interactive=False,
);
</source>
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_hc3n_dirty_chan19.png|200px|thumb|Figure 22: Dirty image for HC3N (SpW 1) channel 19.]]
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_hc3n_psf.png|200px|thumb|Figure 22: PSF for HC3N (SpW 1).]]

It will take a moment to grid the data, and then write out the resulting image products. While we will use the CASA '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.visualization.viewer.html#casatasks.visualization.viewer viewer]''' for the interactive CLEAN procedures below, we use the [https://cartavis.org/ CARTA] application for viewing the resulting image. The CASA viewer is in the process of being deprecated, and while it will be maintained for the near future, CARTA is an excellent tool that already provides a superset of the viewer's functionality.

Figures 22 and 23 show the image and point spread function (PSF), respectively, for channel index 19. This is channel index 1 in the resulting cube since we started from 18 by way of the ''start'' parameter. We can also see that the PSF looks reasonable with the first sidelobes at at the ~15% level and the image quality looks promising. An especially poor PSF may result from miscalculating the weights, but here they look reasonable. While the authors of this guide had good estimates to begin with for the parameters passed to ''tclean'', this would be a good stage to evaluate any changes. For example, depending on how faint or extended the emission is, we may elect to image the data with natural weighting instead of Briggs robust.

===Measuring the image noise===

We next image a subset of channels that are expected to not contain any emission to estimate the per-channel noise from. From Figure 21, we select channel indices 5 through 9. It is useful to know the thermal image noise because several stopping criteria are based on per channel estimates, and for channels with highly extended emission, the noise estimate is likely to be biased high. We can thus set absolute brightness limits to avoid channels that are insufficiently CLEANed.

<source lang="python">
imagename_noise = f"{field_target}_HC3N_noise"
rmtables(f"{imagename_noise}.*")
tclean(
    vis=vis_contsub,
    spw="1",
    imagename=imagename_noise,
    imsize=[300, 300],
    cell="0.4arcsec",
    specmode="cube",
    outframe="LSRK",
    start=5,
    nchan=4,
    restfreq=restfreq_hc3n,
    perchanweightdensity=True,
    pblimit=-0.001,
    weighting="briggs",
    robust=0.5,
    niter=0,
    interactive=False,
);
</source>

Inspecting this cube in CARTA, we can see that there appears to be no emission present. We next use the task '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.information.imstat.html#casatasks.information.imstat imstat]''' to estimate the RMS noise. Note that the noise can also be estimated by creating a region in CARTA and then checking the "statistics" tab. With ''imstat'', the quantities are printed to the logger, and also returned in a variable that we extract the RMS value from below and print it.

<source lang="python">
noise_stats = imstat(imagename=f"{imagename_noise}.image")

rms = noise_stats["rms"][0]
print(f"RMS: {1e3*rms:.6f} mJy")
</source>

This reports a noise value of '''0.97 mJy/beam'''. Note that this value depends on our channel width, which is relevant if one chooses to perform channel averaging on-the-fly in ''tclean''.

===Interactive CLEAN===
Next we image the cube interactively for a few channels. Choose channels with bright, extended emission, since these are likely to require the most attention. We will use these manually CLEANed images as a basis for comparison when evaluating images created using automated techniques. Since the automated techniques require tuning various parameters, these manual images will act as a "ground truth" of sorts. Below we call ''tclean'' with the ''interactive=True'' parameter to image interactively. We also use the RMS calculated above (now set in the user-defined variable ''rms'') to set a threshold at two times the RMS level using the ''threshold'' parameter. Since we know from the dirty image that there is a significant extended emission present, we use the multiscale deconvolver with scale sizes of a delta function (0 pixels), one half-power beamwidth, and three half-power beamwidth. By default ''tclean'' will resume CLEAN from an existing image, if it exists. Errors in CASA can occur when deleting an image that is open in the viewer or open in another process, so we use the '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.manipulation.rmtables.html#casatasks.manipulation.rmtables rmtables]''' task to check whether tables are open in another process before removing them.

<source lang="python">
imagename_interactive = f"{field_target}_HC3N_interactive"
rmtables(f"{imagename_interactive}.*")
tclean(
    vis=vis_contsub,
    spw="1",
    imagename=imagename_interactive,
    imsize=[300, 300],
    cell="0.4arcsec",
    specmode="cube",
    outframe="LSRK",
    start=19,
    nchan=1,
    restfreq=restfreq_hc3n,
    perchanweightdensity=True,
    pblimit=-0.001,
    weighting="briggs",
    robust=0.5,
    deconvolver="multiscale",
    scales=[0,5,15],
    threshold=f"{2*rms:.6f}Jy",
    niter=100_000,
    interactive=True,
);
</source>
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_interactive_chan19_start.png|200px|thumb|Figure 23: Channel 19 for the HC3N cube in the interactive viewer, after adjust the color scheme to the "Hot Metal 2" color scheme using the wrench icon. The white polygon shows the CLEAN mask created after creating and setting a circular region.]]
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_interactive_chan19_end.png|200px|thumb|Figure 23: Channel 19 for the HC3N cube in the interactive viewer, after several rounds of deconvolution. The white polygon shows the CLEAN mask after a few small extensions were added.]]

The '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.visualization.viewer.html#casatasks.visualization.viewer viewer]''' will open when it's ready to start an interactive CLEAN.

'''Important:''' In the green menu on top, '''all polarizations for the clean mask'''. Select either the polygon region tool [[File:Polygon_btn.png]] or the circular region tool. The lines drawn by the region tool will be green, making it difficult to see on the default rainbow color scheme image. The color map can be changed under the Data Display Options: click on the wrench icon or in the top menu, select Data, then select Adjust Data Display. Single clicks can be used to adjust the region and small squares will show anchor points that can be dragged to new positions. For the polygon region tool, single clicks will add new segments with anchor points on the vertices (shown as small green squares). A double click will connect the first and last vertices to create a polygon. Double click within the polygon to add the region to the CLEAN mask, which will be shown in white. To use the circular region tool instead, click and drag the bounding box of the circle over the source and adjust the anchor points on the corners to cover the emission. If you happen to mis-click, set the radio button to "Erase" instead of "Add", and the region will be subtracted from the CLEAN mask.

'''Note''': If an interactive clean is started, and a mask is not created, then ''tclean'' will stop immediately, because in interactive sessions only emission within a mask is deconvolved. This is the opposite of a call to ''tclean'' with ''interactive=False'', where without a mask the entire field of view will be deconvolved in an unrestricted fashion.

To continue with '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.imaging.tclean.html#casatasks.imaging.tclean tclean]''' use one of the Next action buttons in the green area on the Viewer Display GUI: The red "X" [[File:clean-stop.png]] will stop '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.imaging.tclean.html#casatasks.imaging.tclean tclean]''' where it is; the blue arrow [[File:clean-continue.png]] will stop the interactive part of '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.imaging.tclean.html#casatasks.imaging.tclean tclean]''', but continue to clean non-interactively until reaching the stopping niter ('''iterations x cycles''') or threshold, whichever comes first. The green arrow [[File:clean-redo.png]] will clean until it reaches the iterations parameter on the left side of the green area. When the interactive viewer comes back use the tape deck to recheck that the mask encompasses what you think is real emission. If your mouse has a middle button, then by default it controls the image stretch.

For this example, the threshold has been set to two times the RMS via the ''threshold'' parameter to avoid CLEANing too deeply. With a careful CLEAN mask you can CLEAN too close to the thermal noise limit (the actual observed RMS noise limit and not the theoretical one calculated for the proposal, as flagging, weather, etc., can affect what you actually get). It is optimal to CLEAN each channel of a cube to a specific threshold rather than stopping simply by exhausting the ''niter'' parameter, which can leave each channel cleaned to different levels. There are many ways to determine a suitable threshold. One way is to make a dirty image (''niter = 0''), open the cube using the viewer, go to a line free channel, select the box region tool, make a box near the field center about the size of your source, and double click inside.

Continue cleaning by using the green Next Action arrow [[File:clean-redo.png]] until the residual displayed in the viewer looks noise-like. To speed things up, you might change the ''max_cycleniter'' parameter in the viewer. This parameter can also be set in the task command. The residual image shown in Figure 23 was obtained after creating a circular region and two rounds of 100 iterations, extending the region a bit using the polygon region toola nd two rounds of 500 iterations, and then a final round of 5000 iterations. You will notice that in this particular case there are residuals that cannot be cleaned. These residuals are due to the extended, resolved out structure on size scales larger than the array is sensitive to, or the Largest Angular Scale (LAS), that the array is sensitive to can be calculated from the shortest baseline length, and/or potential residual phase and amplitude calibration errors. The resulting restored image is shown in Figure 24.
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_interactive_chan19_restored.png|200px|thumb|Figure 24: Channel 19 for the HC3N cube after interactive deconvolution.]]

Repeat the process for the SiS line using the call below. Note that the emission for this line is in spectral window index 0 and is less extended than the HC3N. The latter has to do with the different excitation situations of the two different lines. The SiS is excited closer to the central star than the HC3N. You may also notice that cleaning this cube takes many more iterations than the HC3N cube, so you may want to increase the iterations in the viewer (at the left in the green area at the top) or just stop before it ends by itself. '''Remember to select All Polarizations.'''

===Automated masking===

One could apply the manual, interactive procedures shown above to all of the channels, but this is generally laborious and time-consuming, especially if one has more than one target and spectral window to CLEAN. We thus use the above files, namely the restored image, the CLEAN mask, and the residual, to help tune the parameters for the automated masking procedures. Extensive parameter explorations have not been made by NRAO staff for EVLA datasets, and so typically some manual exploration and fine-tuning are required to give optimal results.

The masking algorithm we use is referred to as "auto-multithresh" which sets the CLEAN mask based on a combination of peak signal-to-noise in the image and what the current peak sidelobe level is. The image regions generated by these thresholds are then grown to lower signal-to-noise to extend the mask to fainter emission adjacent to more confident detections. This procedure of iteratively growing the mask down to a lower brightness threshold on each cycle roughly mimics the way in which most users generate masks manually: first making bright regions and then expanding the mask as those already CLEANed. Further information on the auto-multithresh algorithm and on tuning the parameters for optimal results can be found in the [https://casaguides.nrao.edu/index.php/Automasking_Guide Automasking Guide]. Note that quite often, good results can be achieved without any CLEAN mask at all, so it is worth trying this at least once before applying the automasking procedures.

The auto-multithresh algorithm tends to require a good amount of tuning on VLA data, so it is recommended to explore parameter combinations on a small number of representative channels (here channel 19) for faster iteration. For compact VLA configurations observing extended emission, part-way between the ALMA 12m and 7m array values offer a good starting point. Typically ''sidelobethreshold'' values are required for VLA observations than ALMA 12m or 7m observations. Below we start with values suitable for jointly imaged ALMA 12m and 7m ALMA observations with a ''noisethreshold=4.0'' and ''sidelobethreshold=1.0'':
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_interactive_chan19_autom_restored.png|200px|thumb|Figure 25: Channel 19 for the HC3N cube after deconvolution with automated CLEAN mask generation.]]

<source lang="python">
imagename_autom = f"{field_target}_HC3N_autom"
rmtables(f"{imagename_autom}.*")
tclean(
    vis=vis_contsub,
    spw="1",
    imagename=imagename_autom,
    imsize=[300, 300],
    cell="0.4arcsec",
    specmode="cube",
    outframe="LSRK",
    start=19,
    nchan=1,
    restfreq=restfreq_hc3n,
    threshold=f"{1*rms:.6f}Jy",
    perchanweightdensity=True,
    pblimit=-0.001,
    weighting="briggs",
    robust=0.5,
    niter=100_000,
    interactive=False,
    # deconvolver
    deconvolver="multiscale",
    scales=[0, 5, 15],
    smallscalebias=0.5,
    # auto-multithresh
    usemask="auto-multithresh",
    noisethreshold=4.0,
    sidelobethreshold=1.0,
    minbeamfrac=0.3,
    lownoisethreshold=1.25,
    negativethreshold=1000.0,
    fastnoise=False,
);
</source>

The results are shown in Figure 25, which shows a sensible mask and a favorable image quality compared to our manually generated run.

===Automated full-cube imaging===

Now that we are happy with our results, we image the full cube. This will be a computationally expensive process, but one that requires little supervision from us now. For larger datasets, it often works well to "touch up" any minor defects in the automated run, such as missing faint extended emission in particularly complex channels, by restarting ''tclean'' on the image with ''interactive=True''. Below we run ''tclean'' the same as above, except excluding the first channel (index 0) by setting ''start=1'' and then image all channels onward by setting ''nchan=-1''. This avoids an issue where the first channel, due to the velocity gridding and interpolation, will contain less data than the other channels and have a very degraded beam, causing issues for imaging the rest of the channels. The run should take approximately 12 major cycles.
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_interactive_chan29_autom_restored.png|200px|thumb|Figure 26: Channel 29 for the HC3N cube after deconvolution with automated CLEAN mask generation.]]
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_interactive_chan10_autom_restored.png|200px|thumb|Figure 27: Channel 10 for the HC3N cube after deconvolution with automated CLEAN mask generation.]]

<source lang="python">
imagename_full = f"{field_target}_HC3N_full"
rmtables(f"{imagename_full}.*")
tclean(
    vis=vis_contsub,
    spw="1",
    imagename=imagename_full,
    imsize=[300, 300],
    cell="0.4arcsec",
    specmode="cube",
    outframe="LSRK",
    start=1,
    nchan=-1,
    restfreq=restfreq_hc3n,
    threshold=f"{1*rms:.6f}Jy",
    perchanweightdensity=True,
    pblimit=-0.001,
    weighting="briggs",
    robust=0.5,
    niter=100_000,
    interactive=False,
    # deconvolver
    deconvolver="multiscale",
    scales=[0, 5, 15],
    smallscalebias=0.5,
    # auto-multithresh
    usemask="auto-multithresh",
    noisethreshold=4.0,
    sidelobethreshold=1.0,
    minbeamfrac=0.3,
    lownoisethreshold=1.25,
    negativethreshold=1000.0,
    fastnoise=False,
);
</source>

We now check the results by viewing (a) line-free channels to see if the masking and deconvolution was too aggressive on "noise spikes" in the image, and (b) checking other channels with strong emission to see how the masks and residuals compared. It is good practice to check both the restored image and residual together along with the CLEAN mask, which can be done in CARTA by selecting "Append" from the "File" menu. In Figure 26 we show another channel (index 29) with complex emission and in Figure 27 we show a channel (index 10) without emission. Both show good quality results without false positives or poor masks.

==Image the Continuum data==

For completeness, we image the continuum for the source as well. Below, we set the parameter ''specmode="mfs"'' in ''tclean'' to create a multi-frequency synthesis image out of all the non-line channels. Since the continuum image is typically quick and straightforward to image at high-frequency and narrow-band, we perform only one interactive CLEAN and create the CLEAN mask manually as above. Since no threshold is set, you will need to stop cleaning when the residual looks noise-like using the red "X" Next Action button [[File:clean-stop.png]] (it will be done when the viewer comes back the second time). The continuum for IRC10216 is comparatively weak but interesting, tracing the photosphere of the AGB star.
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_interactive_cont_restored.png|200px|thumb|Figure 28: Restored continuum image.]]

<source lang="python">
imagename_cont = f"{field_target}_HC3N_cont"
rmtables(tablenames=f"{imagename_cont}.*")
tclean(
    vis=vis_target,
    spw="0~1:3~13;46~60",
    imagename=imagename_cont,
    imsize=[300, 300],
    cell="0.4arcsec",
    specmode="mfs",
    restfreq=restfreq_hc3n,
    perchanweightdensity=True,
    pblimit=-0.001,
    deconvolver="hogbom",
    weighting="briggs",
    robust=0.5,
    niter=100_000,
    interactive=True,
);
</source>

Note that to image the continuum, we use the line-free channels of the data before continuum subtraction, the name of which (''irc10216.ms'') is stored in the user-defined variable ''vis_target''. We also select the line-free channels using a selection with the ''spw'' parameter. Careful observation will show that actually at least two weak lines are detected in our ostensibly line-free channels, so for real scientific applications it would be worthwhile to be more attentive to the channel selection. The resulting restored image is shown in Figure 28.

==Moment maps==

Maps of integrated intensity ("Moment 0"), intensity-weighted velocity ("Moment 1"), and intensity-weighted velocity dispersion ("Moment 2") can be generated using the [https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.analysis.immoments.html#casatasks.analysis.immoments immoments] task. The name "moment" derives from an analogy to [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_(mathematics) statistical moments] in mathematics, although only the moment indices 0, 1, and 2 follow that pattern while the other indices are used to support other statistical metrics (e.g., minimum, median, etc.). Moment maps are especially useful for diagnostic purposes because the collapse (potentially large) three dimensional data cubes into two dimensional images. Moment maps can also be generated in CARTA ([https://carta.readthedocs.io/en/4.0/analysis_tools.html#moment-map-generator link]).

In the example below we calculate Moments 0, 1, and 2 in addition to the maximum value (moment index number 8). To avoid including excess noise in our moment calculation, which is especially problematic for Moments 1 and 2, we threshold the values to only include those above four times the image RMS, as specified by the ''includepix'' parameter below (1e8 is included as stand-in for infinity). Note that thresholding the Moment 0 map can bias it to higher flux values by way of including positive noise spikes and excluding the negatives. For presentation purposes, however, we apply the same thresholds to the Moment 0 map.
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_moment_gallery.png|200px|thumb|Figure 29: Gallery of moment maps with Moment 0 (upper left), Moment 1 (upper right), Moment 2 (lower left), and the maximum (lower right).]]

Below we call the ''immoments'' task that thresholds all values below four times the image RMS and creates the moments map simultaneously by supplying a list of moment map indices (detailed in [https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.analysis.immoments.html#description documentation]). We further sub-select the channels without significant emission to avoid adding undue noise to the statistical quantities. This can be determined by visually inspecting the cube.

<source lang="python">
immoments(
    imagename=f"{imagename_full}.image",
    chans="12~45",
    moments=[0,1,2,8],
    includepix=[4*rms, 1e8],
    outfile=imagename_full,
)
</source>

Note that the warnings about the kernel sampling may be safely ignored. The ''outfile'' parameter i used as the root name for the various images that are written out with file name extensions ''*.integrated'', ''*.coordinate'', ''*.weighted-coordinate'', and ''.maximum''.

[[Image:VLT-HC3Nmom0-SiSmom0-36GHzcont-CASA5.5.0.png|200px|thumb|Figure 30: The VLT V-band image from Le&atilde;o et al. (2006, A&A, 455,187) showing dust rings, overlaid with white HC3N moment 0 contours, black SiS moment 0 contours, and red 36 GHz continuum contours.]]

For fun, you can download the VLT V-band image at http://casa.nrao.edu/Data/EVLA/IRC10216/irc_fors1_dec_header.fits kindly provided by Izan Le&atilde;o and overlay the moment images and 36 GHz continuum (see Figure 30). More information about the dust properties can be found in the article [http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2006A%26A...455..187L Le&atilde;o et al. (2006)]. For using the moment maps as masks or creating masks from them please refer to the [[Masking_images_for_analysis|Masking Images for Analysis]] page.

==Position velocity diagrams==

Position-velocity or "PV" diagrams are diagnostic plots that show the intensity of the emission as a function of position along a "cut" across the image plane (e.g., RA & Dec) and then project the frequency plane (e.g., velocity) into a new image. They are another useful tool for extracting a 2D view from a 3D data cube, which may be difficult to interpret on its own. They are also particularly useful because certain physical systems, such as a disk with Keplerian rotation or a spherically expanding shell, will show unique signatures in a PV diagram. In this section we show how to use the CASA task '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.analysis.impv.html#casatasks.analysis.impv impv]''' to create a PV diagram. One can also use CARTA ([https://carta.readthedocs.io/en/4.0/analysis_tools.html#position-velocity-pv-generator link]) to generate PV diagrams interactively.
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_pv_region_example.png|200px|thumb|Figure 31: Example line-region (cyan) to create a PV diagram from.]]

We first identify the position-slice to use to create the PV diagram from. In this example, for simplicity we open up the restored image in CARTA and create a line-type region and note the start and end image pixel coordinates. Instead of a list of numeric pixel values (e.g., ''[59, 162]''), one may also specify the start and end positions as strings containing the WCS coordinates (e.g., ''["9:47:59.87", "13:16:45.4"]''). Figure 31 shows channel 19 from our restored image and the line region we've drawn in CARTA on top of it, which corresponds to the start x-y pixel ''[59, 162]'' and an end pixel ''[242, 162]''. Note that to create a PV diagram in CARTA, one only needs to click the "PV" button from the list of icons at the top. To generate the PV diagram programmatically in CASA, we call ''impv'' to create the PV diagram as a new image:

<source lang="python">
imagename_pv = f"{field_target}_pv"
rmtables(f"{imagename_pv}.*")
impv(
    imagename=f"{imagename_full}.image",
    outfile=f"{imagename_pv}.image",
    start=[59, 162],
    end=[242, 162],
)
</source>
[[Image:CASA_6.5.3_irc10216_pv_diagram_example.png|200px|thumb|Figure 32: PV diagram along the chosen slice.]]

The resulting image is shown in Figure 32. The HC3N emission observed towards IRC+10216 originates from an (approximately) spherically expanding shell of ejecta. Such motions result in a circular pattern in a PV diagram, which we observe with textbook quality!

== Spectrum Fitting ==

In addition to moment maps and PV-diagrams, we can also use CASA to fit model spectral profiles to the data. This can be done using the task '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.analysis.specfit.html#casatasks.analysis.specfit specfit]'''; '''specfit''' can fit model functions (e.g., Gaussians) to a spectrum averaged over an area or alternatively for each pixel. Below we use CARTA to fit a two-component Gaussian model to a region-averaged spectrum and perform a similar fit using the CASA task '''specfit'''.

We also refer the reader to the wealth of analysis methods available in CARTA. These are described in detail with diagrams in the [https://carta.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ CARTA User Manual]. Methods relevant to spectral line analysis include spectral smoothing, image and spectral model fitting, and querying online databases of molecular and atomic transitions, among others.

=== Fitting an Average Spectrum ===

[[Image:CASA6.5.3-HC3N-spectral-region.png|200px|thumb|Figure 33: Channel 19 (-17.3 km/s) of the HC3N image cube after deconvolution. The cyan line shows the rectangular region used for spectral profile fitting.]]

[[Image:CASA6.5.3-HC3N-spectral-profile.png|200px|thumb|Figure 34: Spectral profile of the HC3N line within the cyan region shown in Fig. 33 alongside a two-component Gaussian fit made with CARTA.]]

To start, we first inspect the spectra in the image. Load the deconvolved HC3N image cube into CARTA and mark a rectangular region as in Figure 33. It is often best to do this for a channel that shows the entire extent of the source, here we select channel index 19. After creating the rectangular region the average profile will be shown in the "Z profile" panel. To perform a quick two-component fit, we follow the instructions [https://carta.readthedocs.io/en/latest/profile_fitting.html profile fitting] section of the CARTA User Manual. In short, select the profile fitting button in the top-right of the spectrum, select the "auto detect" button, and then click the "Fit" button at the bottom of the window (may require scrolling). The resulting fit is shown in Figure 34 (light and dark brown lines).

The profile fitting in CARTA is useful for exploratory analysis, but fitting multiple datasets, or fitting multiple or all of the pixels in a cube, the CASA task '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.analysis.specfit.html#casatasks.analysis.specfit specfit]''' provides a flexible interface. Returning to CARTA, export the region to a CRTF file by navigating to the "Region List" tab and selecting the "export region" button (a small cloud with an upward arrow on top). Name the file ''specfit.crtf''. A thorough description of the region format can be found on the [[CASA Region Format|CASA Region Format]] page.

The outward expansion of IRC+10216's envelope creates a characteristic double-peaked spectral profile, so we will fit a two-component Gaussian model to the spectrum. The scientific merit of this analysis is likely somewhat dubious, but it is a good demonstration for how to use '''specfit'''. A file with initial guesses for the model parameter values to be optimized can be provided via the ''estimates'' parameter (see '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.analysis.specfit.html#casatasks.analysis.specfit specfit]''' for more information). Here we will let CASA determine the start values by itself by setting ''estimates=""'' (i.e., an empty string):

<source lang="python">
fit_results = specfit(
    imagename=f"{imagename_full}.image",
    region="specfit.crtf",
    estimates="",
    ngauss=2,
)
</source>

The fit results are returned in a Python dictionary called ''fit_results'' above and are also printed to the CASA logger.  You should get something similar to the following output, although the results will vary based on the exact coordiantes of your rectangular region to average over and choices made in cleaning the image:

<pre style="background-color: #fffacd;">
Results for component 0:
    Type     : GAUSSIAN
    Peak     : 4.59 +/- 0.38 mJy/beam
    Center   : -16.60 +/- 0.41 km/s
               15.85 +/- 0.40 pixel
    FWHM     : 9.04 +/- 0.99 km/s
               8.77 +/- 0.96 pixel
    Integral : 44.2 +/- 6.1 mJy/beam.km/s
Results for component 1:
    Type     : GAUSSIAN
    Peak     : 3.82 +/- 0.32 mJy/beam
    Center   : -33.98 +/- 0.59 km/s
               32.72 +/- 0.57 pixel
    FWHM     : 13.4 +/- 1.5 km/s
               13.1 +/- 1.5 pixel
    Integral : 54.7 +/- 7.7 mJy/beam.km/s
</pre>
We can see this seems to have caught the two peaks reasonably well.

=== Spectral Fitting pixel by pixel ===

[[Image:CASA5.7.0-F32-irc-amp0.jpg|200px|thumb|Figure 32: Output image of '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.analysis.specfit.html#casatasks.analysis.specfit specfit]''' of the amplitude of the first Gaussian component.]]

Task '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.analysis.specfit.html#casatasks.analysis.specfit specfit]''' can also fit Gaussians to every spectrum in each single spatial pixel. The following command will do this within the '''spectfit.crtf''' region defined above:

<pre style="background-color: #d8bfd8;">
# Interactive CASA
default specfit
inp
imagename='IRC10216_HC3N.cube.image'
region='specfit.crtf'
ngauss=2
multifit=True
amp='fit-amp.image'
center='fit-center.image'
fwhm='fit-fwhm.image'
logresults=True
inp
go
</pre>

<source lang="python">
# Pseudo-interactive CASA
pixfit = specfit(imagename='IRC10216_HC3N.cube.image', region='specfit.crtf', ngauss=2,
         multifit=True,  amp='fit-amp.image', center='fit-center.image', fwhm='fit-fwhm.image')
</source>

In this example, '''[https://casadocs.readthedocs.io/en/v6.7.2/api/tt/casatasks.analysis.specfit.html#casatasks.analysis.specfit specfit]''' will produce three images per Gaussian, images that map the best fit values of the Gauss peaks (amplitudes), velocity centers, and full widths at half maximum. For the first Gaussian, the image to the right displays the amplitude image '''fit.amp.image_0'''.

== Data Pre-processing ==

To perform the same pre-processing as applied to the data in this tutorial, first download the SDM-BDF file ''TDRW0001.sb35770743.eb35774735.58429.44719293981'' under the project code ''TDRW0001'' from the [https://data.nrao.edu NRAO archive], and then run:

<source lang="python">
importasdm(
    asdm="TDRW0001.sb35770743.eb35774735.58429.44719293981",
    vis="TDRW0001.ms",
    ocorr_mode="co",
    with_pointing_correction=True,
    applyflags=True,
    flagbackup=False,
    lazy=True,
)

flagdata(
    vis="TDRW0001.ms",
    mode="shadow",
    flagbackup=False,
);

flagdata(
    vis="TDRW0001.ms",
    mode="quack",
    quackinterval=6.0,
    flagbackup=False,
);

flagdata(
    vis="TDRW0001.ms",
    mode="clip",
    correlation="ABS_ALL",
    clipzeros=True,
    flagbackup=False,
);

mstransform(
    vis="TDRW0001.ms",
    outputvis="TDRW0001_10s.ms",
    timeaverage=True,
    timebin="10s",
    spw="2~3",
    scan="5~59",
    datacolumn="data",
    keepflags=False,
)
</source>
